content.overview: BNS s. 23 — Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will. BNS restatement of IPC 85. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 85. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 23 is the rule on “Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will”. The section provides that nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, is, by reason of intoxication, incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong, or contrary to law; provided that the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 23 exists so that “Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will” has a closed legal test in Chapter III — General Exceptions. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.

The provision in detail
23. Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, is, by reason of intoxication, incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong, or contrary to law; provided that the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will

learningObjectives: Identify the conditions under which involuntary intoxication provides a complete general exception under BNS s. 23.
Examine the mandatory requirement that the intoxicating substance was administered without knowledge or against will.
Apply the cognitive incapacity standard identical to s. 22.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 23 provides that nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, is, by reason of intoxication, incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong, or contrary to law: provided that the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Involuntary intoxication is treated on par with unsoundness of mind. Where a person is involuntarily rendered incapable of rational judgment by fraud, force, or covert administration, moral culpability is absent and criminal liability is excused.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s. 23 (corresponding to IPC s. 85).
Condition precedent: Intoxicating substance must be administered 'without his knowledge' (covert drugging) or 'against his will' (coercion/force).
Cognitive threshold: Intoxication must produce total incapacity to know the nature of the act or that it is wrong or contrary to law.
Temporal requirement: Incapacity must be present at the time of doing the act.
Contrast with voluntary intoxication in s. 24: Self-induced intoxication receives no excuse under s. 23.
essentialIngredients: The person committed an act which constitutes an offence.
At the time of doing it, the person was intoxicated.
The intoxication rendered him completely incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that it was wrong or contrary to law.
The intoxicating substance was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 23 extends the insanity defence to temporary cognitive breakdown caused by involuntary intoxication. The threshold of impairment is high: mild drunkenness or reduced inhibition does not suffice; the person must be rendered incapable of knowing the nature of the act or its moral/legal wrongfulness. Crucially, the origin of the intoxication must be non-voluntary. If the accused voluntarily drank alcohol or consumed drugs, even in larger quantities than intended, s. 23 is strictly barred. The involuntary element must arise from force, duress, medical prescription taken without negligence, or covert spiking of food or drink.
examples: Teaching example (Spiked drink): A guest at a dinner party has a tasteless hallucinogenic substance secretly placed into his fruit juice. He experiences severe delirium, believes he is fighting off wild beasts, and damages property. Section 23 applies because the intoxicant was administered without his knowledge and destroyed his cognitive judgment.

Teaching example (Voluntary consumption): A person voluntarily drinks five pints of liquor, becomes aggressive, and assaults a pedestrian. He cannot plead s. 23 because the intoxication was voluntary; his case falls instead under s. 24.
distinctions: Involuntary intoxication (s. 23) vs Voluntary intoxication (s. 24): Section 23 provides a complete defence if cognitive incapacity is caused without knowledge or against will; Section 24 presumes knowledge even if intoxicated.
Without knowledge vs Against will: 'Without knowledge' covers clandestine poisoning or spiked drinks; 'against will' covers physical coercion or credible threats.
Diminished inhibition vs Total incapacity: Mere excitement or loosened inhibitions does not satisfy the cognitive failure requirement.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who assaulted a colleague after his drink was covertly laced with narcotics can claim exemption under BNS s. 23.
Rule: Section 23 requires involuntary administration (without knowledge/against will) and consequent incapacity to know nature of act or that it was wrong/contrary to law.

Application: Evaluate whether the accused consumed the intoxicant innocently, whether toxicological evidence corroborates spiking, and whether his contemporaneous actions reflect total cognitive incapacity.
Conclusion: If both involuntary administration and requisite cognitive incapacity are established, no offence is committed under s. 23.
